title: Suspicious PowerShell EncodedCommand Execution
description: An encoded PowerShell command was executed. Attackers often use -EncodedCommand to hide malicious activity from command-line logging and evasion of simple string-based detections.
detectionLogic: EventID: 1 AND Image: '*\powershell.exe' AND CommandLine: '* -Enc *' OR CommandLine: '* -EncodedCommand *'
investigationSteps: Retrieve the full command line from the event log.
Decode the Base64 string using a tool like CyberChef or a simple script.
Identify the purpose of the script (e.g., downloading a payload, stealing credentials, lateral movement).
Check the parent process to see if it was a user-initiated action or a scheduled task/service.
remediationSteps: Isolate the affected host if the decoded command is confirmed malicious.
Revoke the credentials used by the account that executed the command.
Terminate the malicious process and remove any persistence mechanisms found (e.g., scheduled tasks, registry keys).
Update detection rules to block similar patterns if they are not legitimate.

title: Brute Force Attempt Against Azure AD
description: Multiple failed login attempts detected for a single user account from different IP addresses within a short timeframe, suggesting a password spraying or brute force attack.
detectionLogic: AppDisplayName: 'Azure Portal' AND ResultType: '50126' (Invalid username or password) AND Count > 10 in 5 minutes
investigationSteps: Review the sign-in logs to identify the source IP addresses and their geolocation.
Check if any login attempts were successful from those IPs.
Assess whether the targeted user is a high-privilege account (e.g., Global Admin).
Verify if the user is traveling or has legitimate reasons for these attempts.
remediationSteps: Enforce Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) for the targeted account immediately.
Temporarily lock the account if a successful login is detected during the attack window.
Block the malicious IP addresses at the conditional access level.
Require a password reset for the affected user.

title: Anomalous DNS Query to Known C2 Domain
description: An internal host made a DNS query for a domain associated with a known Command and Control (C2) infrastructure (e.g., Cobalt Strike, Sliver).
detectionLogic: Query: 'evil-c2-server.com' OR matched against a known threat intelligence feed
investigationSteps: Identify the source internal IP address that made the query.
Correlate the DNS query with network traffic (e.g., HTTP/HTTPS, TCP) to that IP.
Perform an endpoint scan on the source host for malicious processes or files.
Check for other hosts in the network making similar queries.
remediationSteps: Isolate the infected host from the network immediately.
Block the C2 domain and its associated IP addresses at the perimeter firewall/DNS level.
Clean the infection from the host (reimage if necessary).
Analyze the payload to understand the extent of the compromise.

title: Lateral Movement via PsExec
description: The PsExec service was installed and started on a remote host, which is often used by attackers for lateral movement and remote command execution.
investigationSteps: Identify the source host and user account that initiated the PsExec connection.
Check the command executed via PsExec (often visible in Sysmon or EDR logs).
Verify if this is a legitimate administrative action or part of an unauthorized campaign.
Look for other lateral movement tools being used from the same source.
remediationSteps: Disable the PsExec service if not required for legitimate admin tasks.
Revoke the credentials of the user account involved.
Scan both the source and destination hosts for additional indicators of compromise.
Implement restrictive firewall rules to limit RPC/SMB traffic between workstations.

title: AWS S3 Bucket Permissions Change to Public
description: An S3 bucket's access control list (ACL) or policy was modified to allow public read access, potentially exposing sensitive data.
investigationSteps: Identify the IAM user or role that made the change.
Check the contents of the bucket to determine the sensitivity of the data exposed.
Review the justification for making the bucket public.
Check if any data was downloaded while the bucket was public.
remediationSteps: Revert the bucket permissions to private immediately.
Enable 'Block Public Access' at the account or bucket level.
Investigate the IAM entity for signs of compromise (e.g., unusual login times, API calls).
Notify data owners if sensitive information was exposed.

title: Persistence via New Scheduled Task
description: A new scheduled task was created, which might be used by attackers to maintain persistence on a system after a reboot.
investigationSteps: Examine the task name, executable path, and arguments.
Identify the user account that created the task.
Analyze the schedule (e.g., daily at 3 AM, at logon).
Determine if the task's action is malicious (e.g., running a script, beaconing out).
remediationSteps: Delete the suspicious scheduled task.
Investigate how the task was created (e.g., via a compromised account, vulnerability).
Scan the system for other persistence mechanisms (e.g., startup folders, registry keys).
Strengthen Task Scheduler permissions to prevent unauthorized task creation.

title: Detection of Mimikatz Execution
description: Signature or behavioral detection of Mimikatz, a popular tool for harvesting credentials (e.g., LSASS dumping, Golden Ticket creation).
detectionLogic: ProcessName: 'mimikatz.exe' OR CommandArguments: '*sekurlsa::logonpasswords*' OR EDR Behavioral Detection for LSASS access
investigationSteps: Confirm if the detection was a true positive and if it was blocked.
Identify the user who attempted to run the tool and the host machine.
Check for successful credential dumps or ticket creation prior to the detection.
Look for other signs of offensive activity on the host (e.g., lateral movement, reconnaissance).
remediationSteps: Isolate the host immediately if the execution was successful or if the threat is persistent.
Force a password reset for all potentially compromised accounts.
Investigate the source of the Mimikatz binary (e.g., downloaded from web, copied via SMB).
Enable LSA Protection (RunAsPPL) to prevent LSASS memory dumping.

title: Suspicious Login from a New Geolocation
description: A user logged into a system or application from a country they have never visited before, and which is not consistent with their known work location.
detectionLogic: LoginEvent AND Location NOT IN UserKnownLocations
investigationSteps: Check the user's travel history and confirm if they are currently in that location.
Review the IP address for known VPNs or proxy services.
Look for other anomalous activities from the same account (e.g., unusual file access, configuration changes).
Compare the login time with the user's typical working hours.
remediationSteps: Contact the user to verify the login attempt.
Temporarily disable the account or enforce MFA if the login is suspicious.
Revoke active sessions for the account.
Update conditional access policies to block logins from high-risk countries.

title: Large Data Transfer to Cloud Storage
description: An unusually large volume of data was transferred from an internal host to a public cloud storage provider (e.g., Dropbox, Google Drive, Mega.nz).
detectionLogic: Destination: '*.dropbox.com' OR '*.mega.nz' AND ByteCount > 1GB in 1 hour
investigationSteps: Identify the internal host and the user account responsible for the transfer.
Determine what files were being moved if possible (e.g., from endpoint logs, file server audits).
Verify if the transfer was for a legitimate business purpose.
Check if any sensitive or proprietary information was included in the transfer.
remediationSteps: Block access to the cloud storage site if it is not approved for company use.
Isolate the host if unauthorized data exfiltration is suspected.
Conduct a forensic analysis of the host to determine the extent of the data loss.
Implement Data Loss Prevention (DLP) solutions to monitor and block sensitive data transfers.

title: Unauthorized User Added to Domain Admins Group
description: A user account was added to a highly privileged group, such as 'Domain Admins' or 'Enterprise Admins', without proper authorization.
investigationSteps: Identify the user account that made the modification and the user who was added.
Check the change management system for a corresponding approved request.
Verify if this action is part of a legitimate administrative task.
Investigate both the modifying and the modified account for signs of compromise.
remediationSteps: Remove the unauthorized user from the privileged group immediately.
Disable both the modifying and the modified accounts until the investigation is complete.
Audit all recent changes made by these accounts.
Enforce the principle of least privilege and require MFA for all administrative actions.

title: Suspicious Creation of Hidden File in /tmp (Linux)
description: A hidden file (starting with a dot) was created in the /tmp directory, which is a common location for attackers to hide tools or temporary scripts on Linux systems.
investigationSteps: Examine the contents of the hidden file and determine its purpose.
Identify the process and user account that created the file.
Check for other suspicious activities on the host (e.g., network connections, process spawns).
Look for similar files on other Linux servers in the network.
remediationSteps: Delete the suspicious hidden file.
Terminate the process that created the file and investigate its source.
Scan the system for other indicators of compromise.
Configure /tmp with 'noexec' mount option if possible to prevent script execution.

title: Abnormal Volume of API Calls in AWS
description: An IAM entity is making an unusually high number of API calls, which could indicate reconnaissance or automated exfiltration activity.
detectionLogic: EventSource: 'ec2.amazonaws.com' OR 's3.amazonaws.com' AND Count > 500 in 10 minutes for a single UserIdentity
investigationSteps: Identify the IAM user or role and the specific API actions being performed.
Determine if this is part of a legitimate automated script or service.
Check for other anomalous behavior from the same identity (e.g., access from new locations).
Review the impact of the API calls (e.g., resources created, data accessed).
remediationSteps: Temporarily revoke the permissions of the IAM entity.
Investigate the source of the API calls (e.g., an EC2 instance, a developer's workstation).
Rotate the access keys for the affected identity.
Implement service quotas and rate limiting to prevent future occurrences.

title: Creation of New GPO for Script Execution
description: A new Group Policy Object (GPO) was created that includes a startup or login script, which could be used to deploy malware across the domain.
detectionLogic: EventID: 5136 AND ObjectClass: 'groupPolicyContainer' AND AttributeName: 'gPCMachineExtensionNames' contains script extension
investigationSteps: Identify the administrator account that created the GPO.
Review the contents and purpose of the script included in the GPO.
Determine which OUs (Organizational Units) the GPO is linked to.
Verify if this change followed the established change management process.
remediationSteps: Unlink and delete the suspicious GPO immediately.
Investigate the administrator account for compromise.
Scan the systems that were affected by the GPO for signs of malicious activity.
Restrict GPO creation and modification rights to a small, monitored group of admins.

title: Detecting SSH Brute Force from Internal Host
description: An internal Linux host is attempting to log into multiple other internal hosts via SSH using many different usernames or passwords.
detectionLogic: Message: 'Failed password for' AND Count > 5 from the same SourceIP to multiple DestinationIPs
investigationSteps: Identify the source internal IP address and the targeted hosts.
Check if any login attempts were successful.
Analyze the process list on the source host for automated brute-forcing tools (e.g., Hydra, Ncrack).
Determine if the source host itself has been compromised.
remediationSteps: Isolate the source host from the network.
Reset the password and investigate the account used on the source host.
Update firewall rules to restrict SSH access to authorized management IPs only.
Implement Fail2Ban or similar tools to automatically block brute-force attempts.

title: Persistence via DLL Search Order Hijacking
description: A malicious DLL was placed in a directory where a legitimate application will load it instead of the intended system DLL.
detectionLogic: EventID: 7 AND Image: '*\Program Files\*' AND ImageLoaded: '*\Temp\*.dll' OR '*\AppData\*.dll'
investigationSteps: Identify the application that loaded the suspicious DLL.
Examine the malicious DLL file and its associated metadata.
Determine how the DLL was placed in that location (e.g., via a dropper, manual copy).
Check for other signs of compromise on the system (e.g., C2 connections).
remediationSteps: Isolate the affected host.
Remove the malicious DLL and any associated files.
Investigate how the attacker gained initial access to the system.
Use 'Safe DLL Search Mode' and specify absolute paths for DLL loading in internal applications.

title: Large Amount of Emails Sent to External Recipient
description: An internal user account sent an unusually high number of emails to an external email address, potentially indicating data exfiltration or a compromised account used for spam.
detectionLogic: SenderAddress: 'user@company.com' AND RecipientAddress: '*@gmail.com' AND Count > 100 in 1 hour
investigationSteps: Identify the user account and the external recipient email address.
Review the contents of the emails and any attachments.
Check for other signs of account compromise (e.g., login from new location).
Verify if this is a legitimate business activity (e.g., a marketing campaign).
remediationSteps: Temporarily suspend the user's email account or enforce MFA.
Recall the sent emails if possible.
Block the external recipient email address if it is suspicious.
Implement outbound email filtering and data loss prevention (DLP) rules.

title: Creation of New AWS IAM User with AdministratorAccess
description: A new IAM user was created and immediately assigned the 'AdministratorAccess' managed policy, which grants full access to the AWS account.
investigationSteps: Identify the IAM entity that created the new user and assigned the policy.
Verify if this action followed proper approval and IAM guidelines.
Investigate the source IP and location from which the API calls were made.
Determine the purpose of the new administrator account.
remediationSteps: Delete the new IAM user and its associated access keys immediately.
Revoke the permissions of the IAM entity that created the user.
Audit all activities performed by the new administrator account.
Enforce least privilege and use Permission Boundaries to limit the scope of IAM users.

title: Suspicious Use of 'whoami' or 'hostname' in Web Server (Linux)
description: Reconnaissance commands like 'whoami', 'id', or 'hostname' were executed by the web server process (e.g., www-data, apache), which might indicate a web shell or remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability.
detectionLogic: ParentProcess: 'apache2' OR 'nginx' AND ProcessName: 'whoami' OR 'id' OR 'hostname'
investigationSteps: Identify the specific web application or page that triggered the command.
Analyze the web server access logs for suspicious requests around the time of execution.
Search for web shells or malicious files on the web server.
Check for network connections initiated by the web server process to external IPs.
remediationSteps: Isolate the web server from the network.
Remove any web shells or malicious code found.
Patch the vulnerable web application or server software.
Restrict the permissions of the web server process and implement a Web Application Firewall (WAF).

title: Persistence via AppInit_DLLs Registry Key
description: A new DLL was added to the AppInit_DLLs registry key, which causes it to be loaded into every process that links with User32.dll.
investigationSteps: Identify the DLL being loaded and its file location.
Determine which user or process modified the registry key.
Analyze the malicious DLL for its capabilities.
Check for other signs of persistence and lateral movement on the system.
remediationSteps: Remove the suspicious DLL from the AppInit_DLLs registry key.
Delete the DLL file from the system.
Isolate the host and investigate the root cause of the compromise.
Monitor this registry key for future unauthorized modifications.

title: Unauthorized Access to Key Vault (Azure)
description: An unauthorized user or application attempted to access or retrieve secrets from an Azure Key Vault.
investigationSteps: Identify the user or application that attempted the access and its IP address.
Check the Key Vault access policies and RBAC roles for the identity.
Determine if this was a misconfiguration or a malicious reconnaissance attempt.
Review the impact if any secrets were successfully accessed before being blocked.
remediationSteps: Review and tighten Key Vault access policies.
Enable 'Private Link' to restrict Key Vault access to internal networks.
Investigate the identity for signs of compromise.
Rotate any secrets that might have been compromised.

title: Data Breach: Exfiltration via DNS Tunneling
description: Large volume of DNS queries with high-entropy subdomains, indicating data being exfiltrated via DNS tunneling (e.g., iodine, dnscat2).
detectionLogic: QueryLength > 50 AND UniqueSubdomains > 1000 in 1 hour from a single SourceIP
investigationSteps: Identify the internal host making the excessive DNS queries.
Analyze the payload of the DNS queries for encoded data.
Identify the destination authoritative DNS server.
Check for associated malicious processes on the source host.
remediationSteps: Isolate the host immediately.
Block the destination domain and nameserver IP.
Analyze the host for persistent tunneling software.
Implement DNS inspection and rate limiting.

title: Ransomware: Mass File Encryption Activity
description: Rapid succession of file renames and writes with known ransomware extensions (e.g., .locked, .crypt, .wanna).
detectionLogic: FileExtension IN KnownRansomwareExtensions AND FileWriteCount > 50 in 1 minute
investigationSteps: Identify the process and user responsible for the file changes.
Determine the scope of the encryption (which drives/folders).
Look for the ransom note file creation.
Check for lateral movement from the infected host.
remediationSteps: Kill the malicious process immediately.
Isolate the host from the network and shared drives.
Disable the compromised user account.
Restore files from the latest verified backup.

title: Account Takeover: MFA Fatigue Attack (MFA Spamming)
description: Multiple MFA push notifications sent to a user followed by a successful login, suggesting the user eventually approved a malicious request due to fatigue.
detectionLogic: MFAPushSentCount > 5 AND MFAStatus: 'Approved' within a short interval
investigationSteps: Contact the user to verify if they intentionally approved the request.
Check the source IP and location of the initial login attempt.
Review logs for any actions taken immediately after the successful MFA.
Identify if the login bypasses Conditional Access policies.
remediationSteps: Revoke all active sessions for the user.
Reset the user's password immediately.
Switch to hardware-based MFA (FIDO2) or number matching for push.
Review and clean up any unauthorized changes in the account.

title: PC Takeover: Unauthorized AnyDesk Connection
description: A connection from an unknown external IP to the AnyDesk service on a corporate workstation, often used for remote access takeover.
investigationSteps: Identify the user currently logged into the PC.
Check if AnyDesk was authorized for this specific task.
Look for files downloaded or transferred during the AnyDesk session.
Analyze the external IP for reputation and geolocation.
remediationSteps: Terminate the AnyDesk session and process.
Uninstall unauthorized remote access software.
Reset the user's local and domain credentials.
Implement a policy to block unauthorized remote access ports at the firewall.

title: Domain Takeover: DCSync Attack Detected
description: A non-domain controller account is requesting replication of sensitive AD data, indicating a DCSync attack to steal password hashes.
detectionLogic: EventID: 4662 AND ObjectType: 'domainDNS' AND AccessMask: '0x100' (Replicating Directory Changes All)
investigationSteps: Identify the source account and host machine.
Confirm if the account has legitimate replication privileges (highly unlikely for users).
Check for recent privilege escalation on the source host.
Monitor for lateral movement or 'Golden Ticket' usage following this event.
remediationSteps: Isolate the source host immediately.
Disable the compromised account (likely a highly privileged service account).
Reset the KRBTGT password twice to invalidate all existing Kerberos tickets.
Perform a full forensic audit of the Active Directory environment.

title: Ransomware: Shadow Copy Deletion
description: Execution of 'vssadmin delete shadows' or 'wmic shadowcopy delete', a precursor to ransomware encryption to prevent local recovery.
investigationSteps: Identify the parent process that spawned the command (often a malicious script).
Check if encryption has already started on the host.
Identify the user account under which the command was executed.
Search for other ransomware-related tools on the system (e.g., cleaners, scanners).
remediationSteps: Isolate the host immediately.
Terminate any suspicious running processes.
Verify the integrity of backups and offline storage.
Restore the host from a known good state.

title: Data Breach: Large SQL Dump via Internal Host
description: An unusually large number of rows exported or a 'SELECT *' on a sensitive table (e.g., Users, CreditCards) by an unusual user.
investigationSteps: Verify if the query was part of a legitimate reporting task.
Identify where the resulting data was sent (e.g., to a local file, over the network).
Check the credentials used and if they were recently rotated.
Look for other signs of reconnaissance on the database server.
remediationSteps: Disable the compromised database user account.
Block the IP of the host that initiated the query.
Review and restrict database permissions (implement RBAC).
Enable data masking for sensitive fields in the database.

title: Account Takeover: Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) Cookie Theft
description: A session cookie for a critical application was used from an IP address that differs significantly from the initial authentication IP, suggesting cookie theft.
detectionLogic: SessionID: 'Matched' AND IPAddress: 'Changed' AND Geolocation: 'Impossible Travel'
investigationSteps: Review the proxy logs for any suspicious domains visited before the cookie was stolen (e.g., look-alike domains).
Identify the user account and the applications accessed with the stolen cookie.
Check if MFA was bypassed or already completed by the attacker.
Assess the level of access granted by the stolen session.
remediationSteps: Invalidate all active sessions for the affected user account.
Reset the user's password and MFA tokens.
Implement Token Binding or IP-bound sessions where supported.
Educate the user on phishing and suspicious URL verification.
logsNeeded: Azure AD Sign-in Logs (Sign-in risky events)

title: PC Takeover: Unauthorized RDP from Public IP
description: Successful RDP login to a workstation directly from a public IP address, bypassing the corporate VPN.
detectionLogic: EventID: 4624 AND LogonType: 10 AND SourceIP NOT IN InternalRange
investigationSteps: Identify the user who logged in and the workstation involved.
Check if the workstation was intentionally exposed to the internet (misconfiguration).
Analyze the activities performed during the RDP session.
Look for other workstations exposed in a similar manner.
remediationSteps: Terminate the RDP session immediately.
Block RDP (Port 3389) at the external firewall.
Enforce VPN-only RDP access.
Disable the compromised user account and reset their password.

title: Domain Takeover: Golden Ticket Usage detected via 4624/4672
description: A logon event where the user claims to be a highly privileged account but the TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket) has a suspiciously long lifetime or missing fields, indicating a Golden Ticket.
detectionLogic: EventID: 4624 AND TargetUserName: 'Administrator' AND AuthenticationPackage: 'Kerberos' AND TicketLifetime > 10 hours
investigationSteps: Identify the host where the Golden Ticket was used.
Trace the activity back to the initial compromise point.
Check for DCSync activity that could have preceded the ticket creation.
Identify all resources accessed using this fraudulent ticket.
remediationSteps: Isolate all affected systems.
Reset the KRBTGT account password twice immediately.
Perform a full rebuild of the compromised forest if necessary.
Implement Tiered Administration to protect highly privileged accounts.

title: Data Breach: Github Repository Leaking Secrets
description: A commit to a public or private company repository contains hardcoded API keys, database credentials, or AWS secret keys.
investigationSteps: Identify the developer who made the commit.
Verify the validity of the leaked secret (is it active?).
Determine if the secret has been used by an external entity since the leak.
Check if the secret grants access to production environments.
remediationSteps: Revoke and rotate the leaked secret immediately.
Remove the secret from the Git history (using BFG Repo-Cleaner or git-filter-repo).
Investigate associated logs for unauthorized access using the secret.
Implement pre-commit hooks to prevent future leaks.

title: Ransomware: Cobalt Strike Beaconing Detected
description: Network traffic pattern consistent with Cobalt Strike beaconing (periodic GET/POST requests with specific metadata headers), often used by ransomware actors for C2.
detectionLogic: TrafficPattern: 'Periodic' AND UserAgent: 'Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; MSIE 9.0; Windows NT 6.1; Trident/5.0)' AND PayloadEntropy: High
investigationSteps: Identify the infected host and the process responsible for the traffic.
Scan the host for Cobalt Strike artifacts (e.g., reflective loaders in memory).
Determine the initial infection vector (e.g., spear-phishing, RDP exploit).
Check for lateral movement or data staging.
remediationSteps: Isolate the host from the network.
Kill the malicious process and remove persistence.
Block the C2 IP and domain at the perimeter.
Perform memory forensics to identify additional payloads.

title: Account Takeover: Session Hijacking via Malicious Browser Extension
description: A browser extension is captured sending session cookies or keystrokes to an external domain.
investigationSteps: Identify the malicious extension ID and name.
Determine how the extension was installed (e.g., user-installed, side-loaded).
Identify which web accounts were accessed during the session.
Scan the host for other malware.
remediationSteps: Remove the malicious browser extension.
Clear browser cache and cookies.
Invalidate all web sessions and reset passwords for affected accounts.
Implement a policy to restrict browser extension installations.

title: PC Takeover: Reverse Shell established via Python
description: A python process spawned a cmd.exe or /bin/sh with an active network connection, typical of a reverse shell.
investigationSteps: Analyze the Python script that initiated the shell.
Identify the remote IP address and its reputation.
Check what commands were executed through the reverse shell.
Identify how the Python script was initially executed (e.g., web shell, scheduled task).
remediationSteps: Kill the Python process and the child shell.
Isolate the host and block the remote IP.
Remove the malicious script and any persistence mechanisms.
Review and restrict execution of scripting languages for non-developers.

title: Domain Takeover: AD CS Certificate Template Misconfiguration exploited
description: An attacker requested a certificate for a highly privileged user (e.g., Domain Admin) using a misconfigured template (ESC1/ESC8).
detectionLogic: EventID: 4886 AND TemplateName: 'VulnerableTemplate' AND Requester: 'StandardUser' AND SAN: 'Administrator'
investigationSteps: Identify the user account that requested the certificate.
Verify if the certificate was used for authentication (Event ID 4624).
Review AD CS templates for misconfigurations (e.g., 'Supply in request' allowed for SAN).
Identify any other certificates issued using the same vulnerable template.
remediationSteps: Revoke the fraudulent certificate immediately.
Disable the vulnerable AD CS template or correct its permissions.
Isolate the compromised user account.
Monitor for logons using the revoked certificate thumbprint.

title: Data Breach: Exfiltration via MEGA.nz Desktop App
description: Unauthorized installation and use of MEGA.nz desktop sync client on a server containing sensitive data.
investigationSteps: Identify the user who installed the client.
Check which folders were synced to the MEGA cloud.
Analyze the network logs for total data transferred.
Determine if the user was authorized to use personal cloud storage.
remediationSteps: Terminate the MEGAsync process and uninstall the software.
Block access to MEGA.nz at the firewall/proxy.
Conduct a data loss assessment to see what was synced.
Discipline or retrain the user based on security policy.

title: Ransomware: LockBit 3.0 (LockBit Black) behavioral pattern
description: Detection of LockBit 3.0 specific behaviors: disabling security tools, deleting logs, and high-speed encryption.
investigationSteps: Confirm the presence of the LockBit binary (often randomly named).
Identify the ransom note (often named 'README.txt' or similar with a custom extension).
Check for exfiltration activity prior to encryption (Double Extortion).
Identify the compromised entry point (e.g., VPN, Phishing).
remediationSteps: Isolate the host immediately.
Shut down affected servers to prevent further encryption if not already complete.
Consult with incident response experts and legal counsel.
Do NOT pay the ransom unless absolutely necessary (consult law enforcement).

title: Account Takeover: Password Spraying against O365
description: A single external IP address attempting to log into hundreds of different user accounts with a small set of common passwords.
detectionLogic: Source: 'External IP' AND UserCount > 50 AND FailedLoginCount > 100
investigationSteps: Identify if any accounts were successfully compromised during the spray.
Check the IP address reputation (VPN, TOR, known malicious proxy).
Monitor successful logins from that IP for anomalous activity.
Determine the password list used if possible.
remediationSteps: Block the malicious IP at the tenant level.
Force a password reset for any users with successful logins from that IP.
Enforce MFA for all users if not already enabled.
Monitor the environment for lateral movement from potentially compromised accounts.

title: PC Takeover: VNC Server started by unusual process
description: A VNC server (e.g., WinVNC, TightVNC) was launched by a non-standard parent process like a web browser or a temporary directory executable.
investigationSteps: Identify the VNC configuration (port, password, allowed IPs).
Check for active connections to the VNC server.
Analyze how the VNC binary was dropped on the system.
Determine if the user was aware of the VNC installation.
remediationSteps: Kill the VNC process and delete the binary.
Uninstall any associated VNC services.
Isolate the host and scan for other remote access tools.
Review firewall rules to block common VNC ports (5900+).

title: Domain Takeover: PrintNightmare Exploit Attempt (CVE-2021-34527)
description: Attempt to load a malicious driver via the Print Spooler service, potentially granting SYSTEM privileges and domain control.
investigationSteps: Identify the source of the print request and the user account.
Verify if the Spooler service is patched against PrintNightmare.
Check for the creation of new files in C:\Windows\System32\spool\drivers.
Look for privilege escalation activity following the event.
remediationSteps: Stop and disable the Print Spooler service on all Domain Controllers.
Apply the latest Microsoft security updates.
Isolate the host that initiated the exploit attempt.
Remove any unauthorized printer drivers from the system.

title: Data Breach: Exfiltration of Email PST/OST files
description: Large .pst or .ost files (Outlook data files) being copied to a USB drive or uploaded to a personal cloud account.
detectionLogic: FilePath: '*.pst' OR '*.ost' AND Action: 'Copy' AND Target: 'RemovableMedia'
investigationSteps: Identify the user and the workstation.
Determine the sensitivity of the emails contained in the data files.
Check if this is a standard archiving procedure or unauthorized theft.
Verify if the destination storage is company-approved.
remediationSteps: Block the USB transfer and notify the user.
Isolate the workstation if the upload was to an unauthorized cloud service.
Revoke the user's access to sensitive email data.
Implement DLP rules to block the movement of Outlook data files.

title: Ransomware: Hive Ransomware Indicators detected
description: Detection of Hive ransomware strings, ransom notes ('HOW_TO_DECRYPT.txt'), and the '.hive' file extension.
investigationSteps: Identify the compromised user account (often via RDP brute force).
Check for lateral movement to critical servers (ESXi, SQL).
Look for exfiltration via tools like Rclone.
Assess the extent of the damage across the network.
remediationSteps: Isolate affected servers and workstations immediately.
Disable compromised credentials.
Consult with legal and security specialists for extortion negotiation if necessary.
